claims.claim: Scenario manifests use apiVersion promptkit.altairalabs.ai/v1alpha1 (repeated in every example)
kind is Scenario
metadata.name identifies the scenario
metadata.tags is a list of strings used for filtering
spec.task_type is a field that links the scenario to a prompt configuration
spec.fixtures is a map of test-specific data available to the scenario
spec.turns is a list of conversation turns
turn role accepts the value user
turn content is a string field holding the user message
a turn accepts an assertions list
content_includes is a registered assertion type
content_includes takes a params.patterns list of strings
assertion params accept a message field, and it is optional
task_type connects the scenario to its prompt configuration
content_matches is a registered assertion type (used with params.pattern at line 76)
content_matches params.pattern is a Go regular expression that accepts the inline (?i) flag
fixtures are the mechanism that sets up context before a turn (Arrange phase)
{{fixtures.long_text}} interpolates a fixture into turn content
Example defines fixture long_patterns but line 228 references fixtures.long_text (name mismatch, example is inconsistent)
Multi-language example: llm_judge assertion with judge_provider openai/gpt-4o-mini under a second scenario entry (scenario list form)
a context block can sit at scenario level and holds named state (user, current_session)
context values are passed to the LLM so it can use them in its response
conversation history is implicit: earlier turns are carried into later turns' requests
a fixtures entry can be a multi-line text block scalar (long_text)
a turn accepts a name field
${fixtures.premium_user} is the interpolation syntax inside a context block
llm_judge accepts a params.criteria string
llm_judge accepts judge_provider in the form openai/gpt-4o-mini and this provider is registered
content_matches patterns support negative lookahead (?!...)
spec.description is a field on the scenario spec
content_includes params.patterns accepts a bare string instead of a list
a turn accepts a context block (booking_state)
provider mock is a usable provider in Arena configs
providers can be given as a list of bare model names such as gpt-4o, claude and gemini
a turn accepts a providers list (Full Conversation Flow example)
turns can be written as a count placeholder such as [10 multi-turn exchanges]
metadata accepts version, last_updated, author and changelog keys
a scenario accepts a deprecated: true field
a scenario accepts a deprecated_reason field
a scenario accepts a skip: true field
Arena has no deprecated or skip fields and retired scenarios are managed with labels or removal
a top-level templates key defines reusable blocks in an Arena config
YAML anchors (&name) and aliases (*name) are parsed in scenario files
the YAML merge key << is honoured when loading a scenario
scenario files may live in nested subdirectories such as smoke/ and customer-support/
link target /arena/explanation/testing-philosophy/ exists
link target /arena/explanation/validation-strategies/ exists
link target /arena/explanation/provider-comparison/ exists
link target /arena/how-to/scenarios/write-scenarios/ exists
Special characters example is a valid Scenario manifest (its indentation is broken, and tags, turns and name sit at the wrong level)
Multi-turn Conversation Flow example is a valid Scenario (tags is indented under spec and turns is not a sibling of task_type)
State transitions example is a valid Scenario (blank indented block between description and turns)
Branch testing example is valid YAML (turns key appears twice in a row)
Branch B example repeats the turns key under the same parent (duplicate key)
Inherited turn example: merge key <<: *support_base is placed on a turn that also has its own name and nested turns list
God Scenarios anti-pattern example has a duplicate turns key
Missing Context anti-pattern example has a duplicate turns key
Cost example uses providers and turns as lists on a turn, which Arena would not run as written
